section_summary: This section traces Japan’s currency and gold policies from the lifting of the gold embargo in 1930 through the financial pressures of the war in China in 1938. It covers proposals to devalue the yen, gold purchase prices and shipments, exchange-rate policy, replacement coinage, and the use of gold reserves to finance imports for export production.

people.name: Neville
people.role: United States diplomatic officer in Japan

people.name: Castle
people.role: United States diplomatic officer in Japan

people.name: Henry Morgenthau Jr.
people.role: United States Secretary of the Treasury

people.name: Hall-Patch
people.role: Financial Adviser to the British Embassy in China

subfiles.title: File note on removal of gold embargo
subfiles.about: Points to a despatch reporting gold withdrawals after the embargo was lifted.
subfiles.summary: About ¥100,000 in gold was reportedly withdrawn on the first day.

subfiles.title: File note on gold exports after the embargo
subfiles.about: Points to a discussion of gold exports and Japan’s financial stability.
subfiles.summary: Records ¥40.8 million in gold exports by January’s end; observers saw no immediate danger.

subfiles.title: Discussion of gold exports and financial stability
subfiles.about: Explains why observers were unconcerned by Japan’s early gold outflow.
subfiles.summary: Gold exports reached ¥40.8 million after the ban ended. Observers cited seasonal demand for dollar drafts and unused stabilization credits in New York and London.

subfiles.title: File note on falling commodity prices
subfiles.about: Points to a despatch on prices following the renewed gold embargo.
subfiles.summary: Commodity prices fell despite the Seiyūkai government’s advertised inflation policy.

subfiles.title: File note on commodity prices and the yen
subfiles.about: Points to a despatch on continued price declines.
subfiles.summary: Commodity prices kept falling despite a slight decline in the yen’s exchange value.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on proposals to devalue the yen
subfiles.about: Summarizes Tokyo’s report on devaluation proposals and farmers’ debts.
subfiles.summary: Farm debt prompted proposals to cut the yen’s value by law or inflation. Opposition stopped a direct resolution, but the Diet expanded the Bank of Japan’s authority to issue notes.

subfiles.title: Proposals for devaluation of the Japanese yen
subfiles.about: Reports competing proposals to reduce the yen’s gold value or inflate its currency.
subfiles.summary: Grew links devaluation proposals to severe farm and small-business debt. A Seiyūkai plan to reduce the yen’s gold value to one-fifth met opposition from newspapers, the minority party, and ministers. A gradual inflation proposal attracted less interest, but a new law greatly increased the Bank of Japan’s permitted fiduciary note issue, suggesting further inflation attempts.

subfiles.title: File note on proposed yen devaluation
subfiles.about: Points to a despatch on the rejected devaluation proposal.
subfiles.summary: The proposal arose from farmers’ debts and was dropped after strong opposition.

subfiles.title: Proposal to devalue the yen
subfiles.about: Describes two proposed approaches to yen devaluation.
subfiles.summary: A proposed legislative reduction of the yen’s gold parity was abandoned after opposition. An inflationary approach appeared more likely in light of Diet legislation.

subfiles.title: File note on a Japanese open gold market
subfiles.about: Points to a report on whether Japan would create an open gold market.
subfiles.summary: Indexes a report on government gold-market plans.

subfiles.title: Japanese government plans regarding an open gold market
subfiles.about: Reports that officials disclosed no plan to establish an open gold market.
subfiles.summary: Informal inquiries yielded no firm information. The government continued buying producers’ gold at fixed prices below likely free-market prices.

subfiles.title: File note on increased gold purchase price
subfiles.about: Points to a despatch explaining Japan’s higher price for newly mined gold.
subfiles.summary: Indexes the November 24 increase and its stated reasons.

subfiles.title: Price of gold
subfiles.about: Explains Japan’s increase in its purchase price for newly mined gold.
subfiles.summary: The price rose from ¥8.88 to ¥9.94 per momme to curb smuggling and attract hoarded gold.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about Japan’s gold purchase price
subfiles.about: Requests an explanation of the recent rise in Japan’s gold buying price.
subfiles.summary: The Treasury asks the Embassy for information.

subfiles.title: Explanation of the increased gold price
subfiles.about: Explains the new purchase price and its relation to Japan’s gold policy.
subfiles.summary: Japan raised its price to ¥11.09 per momme to encourage sales to the government and deter smuggling. The Embassy saw no special implication for the yen’s eventual gold value.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of gold-price telegram to Treasury
subfiles.about: Sends confirmation copies of Tokyo’s April 9 telegram.
subfiles.summary: Encloses three copies of Grew’s report on the exchange and monetary situation.

subfiles.title: Correction to Japan’s gold purchase price
subfiles.about: Corrects the announced price for gold.
subfiles.summary: The Bank of Japan revised the price from ¥11.09 to ¥11.06 per momme after finding a calculation error.

subfiles.title: Recent decline in exchange of Japanese currency
subfiles.about: Records Treasury concern about the yen’s fall against sterling.
subfiles.summary: Officials prepared inquiries to Tokyo and Dairen after the yen continued falling when sterling stabilized.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about the yen–sterling rate
subfiles.about: Asks whether Japan resisted the yen’s recent decline.
subfiles.summary: Requests information on the fall and Japanese exchange policy.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about exchange purchases at Dairen
subfiles.about: Asks about heavy purchases of Chinese exchange at Dairen.
subfiles.summary: Seeks to determine whether purchases were speculative or tied to the Chinese Eastern Railway.

subfiles.title: Report on Chinese exchange purchases at Dairen
subfiles.about: Relays the Dairen consul’s account of heavy Shanghai-exchange purchases.
subfiles.summary: Foreign banks considered the purchases largely speculative; railway payments were only a potential factor.

subfiles.title: Report on yen–sterling exchange policy
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese efforts to prevent a sharp yen decline.
subfiles.summary: Bank rates suggested intervention near one shilling two pence per yen, with no apparent change in overall exchange policy.

subfiles.title: Treasury letter on yen exchange and Dairen purchases
subfiles.about: Summarizes Embassy responses to Treasury’s exchange-rate inquiries.
subfiles.summary: The letter reports apparent Japanese support for the yen–sterling rate and no evident policy change. Dairen’s Chinese-exchange buying appeared mainly speculative.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on depreciation of Japanese yen
subfiles.about: Assesses the competitive effect of yen depreciation on Japanese exports.
subfiles.summary: The yen had fallen 42.3 percent against the dollar, but rising Japanese raw-material costs reduced the likely export advantage. The memorandum estimates Japan’s gain in the American market at no more than 25–30 percent.

subfiles.title: File note on Leith-Ross in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Points to a telegram on the British financial expert’s visit.
subfiles.summary: Notes no evidence of negotiations with Japanese officials.

subfiles.title: Leith-Ross’s visit to Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports on Leith-Ross’s contacts and Japanese press reaction.
subfiles.summary: Leith-Ross made courtesy calls but apparently held no negotiations. Press criticism of British economic policy suggested little willingness to discuss concrete financial proposals.

subfiles.title: File note on financial trends
subfiles.about: Points to a despatch on Japan’s financial trends.
subfiles.summary: Indexes a short assessment of markets, prices, trade, and the yen.

subfiles.title: Financial trends
subfiles.about: Summarizes recent Japanese market and price movements.
subfiles.summary: Money was easy; shares and commodity prices rose; industry and trade remained satisfactory.

subfiles.title: Proposed revaluation of Bank of Japan specie
subfiles.about: Reports a plan to revalue specie and create a gold and exchange fund.
subfiles.summary: Proposed legislation would revalue Bank of Japan specie and transfer an estimated ¥590 million net book profit to a special account. The account would fund gold purchases, specie exports, and yen stabilization, though observers doubted it would improve the yen’s underlying position.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of specie-revaluation telegram
subfiles.about: Forwards copies of Tokyo’s specie-revaluation report.
subfiles.summary: Encloses six copies of the July 21 telegram.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding Chinese aide-mémoire on bank notes
subfiles.about: Forwards China’s protest over proposed Yokohama Specie Bank notes in Tientsin.
subfiles.summary: Suggests informing American banks without comment.

subfiles.title: Chinese aide-mémoire on Yokohama Specie Bank notes
subfiles.about: Requests action against circulation of Yokohama Specie Bank notes.
subfiles.summary: China says the proposed issue would disturb its money market and asks that foreign banks refuse the notes.

subfiles.title: Chinese-language enclosure
subfiles.about: Original-language enclosure accompanying the translated aide-mémoire.
subfiles.summary: The OCR preserves only a brief Chinese fragment.

subfiles.title: Japan’s shipments of gold
subfiles.about: Estimates Japan’s remaining gold after October shipments to the United States.
subfiles.summary: More than ¥90 million had been shipped; the memorandum estimates at most ¥250 million remained readily available.

subfiles.title: Suggested embargo against Japanese gold
subfiles.about: Records Treasury objections to refusing purchases of Japanese gold.
subfiles.summary: Archie Lochhead argues Japan could sell gold indirectly through other markets and that an embargo could undermine gold’s reserve value. He doubts other countries would join such a measure.

subfiles.title: On the matter of ceasing gold purchases from Japan
subfiles.about: Assesses the legal and practical effect of ending Japanese gold purchases.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum describes a purchase ban as discretionary policy. It concludes unilateral action would be ineffective, while coordinated action would still leave Japan possible ways to use its gold.

subfiles.title: Gold shipments from Kobe in April and May
subfiles.about: Lists recent gold shipments from Kobe.
subfiles.summary: Reports four shipments totaling ¥75 million between April 20 and May 11.

subfiles.title: Planned May 25 gold shipment
subfiles.about: Reports a planned gold shipment from Kobe.
subfiles.summary: The Bank of Japan expected to ship ¥20 million aboard Hokuriku Maru.

subfiles.title: Ikeda’s financial and trade policy
subfiles.about: Analyzes the new Finance Minister’s policies on gold, imports, exports, and savings.
subfiles.summary: Ikeda favored conserving reserves, shipping newly mined gold, and easing selected import restrictions to support exports. The Embassy identifies tension between lower interest rates for industry and higher rates for savings. It expects efforts to reduce domestic prices and improve access to raw materials.

subfiles.title: Consular report on June 21 gold shipment
subfiles.about: Relays Kobe consular invoice details for gold sent to San Francisco.
subfiles.summary: Reports 147,787.953 troy ounces shipped aboard Tatsuta Maru, invoiced at ¥17.7 million.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Kobe gold-shipment telegram
subfiles.about: Forwards the telegram reporting Kobe’s June 21 gold shipment.
subfiles.summary: Encloses one copy of the Shanghai telegram.

subfiles.title: Bank of Japan report on June 21 shipment
subfiles.about: Confirms a gold shipment from Kobe to the United States.
subfiles.summary: Reports about ¥17 million in gold aboard Tatsuta Maru.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Tokyo gold-shipment telegram
subfiles.about: Forwards Tokyo’s confirmation of the June shipment.
subfiles.summary: Encloses six copies of telegram No. 430.

subfiles.title: File memorandum on new subsidiary currency
subfiles.about: Highlights a consular report on Japan’s replacement coinage.
subfiles.summary: Japan was replacing nickel and silver currency with less valuable materials.

subfiles.title: New subsidiary currency of Japan
subfiles.about: Describes Japan’s new coins and note and the metal-saving purpose of the change.
subfiles.summary: The report specifies new 10-, 5-, and 1-sen coins and a 50-sen note. The change replaces nickel and silver currency and applies in Japan’s colonies. Richardson estimates recoverable nickel coinage at roughly one year’s normal nickel use outside coinage.

subfiles.title: Proposal to ship Bank of Japan gold reserves
subfiles.about: Reports advisers’ support for shipping reserves to fund raw-material imports.
subfiles.summary: Cabinet approval was still required before action.

subfiles.title: Cabinet approval of reserve-gold credit
subfiles.about: Reports release of specie reserves for a revolving foreign-exchange credit.
subfiles.summary: The Cabinet approved shipping ¥300 million in reserves to finance raw materials for export goods, with export bills replenishing the fund. The Embassy notes the strain on other gold holdings and doubts that foreign demand for Japanese goods will rise substantially.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of reserve-gold telegram
subfiles.about: Paraphrases the Cabinet’s decision to use gold reserves for export production.
subfiles.summary: The paraphrase describes the ¥300 million revolving credit, concern about depleted gold holdings, and the Finance Minister’s view that productive use of specie need not endanger the yen.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of reserve-gold telegram paraphrase
subfiles.about: Forwards the paraphrase of Grew’s July 20 telegram.
subfiles.summary: Encloses one copy for the Treasury.

subfiles.title: Hall-Patch’s views on North China and Japanese finance
subfiles.about: Relays a British adviser’s assessment of trade, currency, sanctions, and credits.
subfiles.summary: Hall-Patch discusses the Federal Reserve Bank in North China, falling Chinese currency, and pressure on Japanese finance. He believes coordinated sanctions could force Japan to terms and questions reported petroleum credits to Japan, asking Washington to verify them.

subfiles.title: Bank of Japan reserve decline
subfiles.about: Reports the published reduction in Bank of Japan specie reserves.
subfiles.summary: The stated reserve fell by ¥300 million to about ¥501 million.

subfiles.title: Forwarding the Emergency Currency Law and ordinances
subfiles.about: Forwards translations of Japan’s Emergency Currency Law and related ordinances.
subfiles.summary: The measures conserve metals through subsidiary coins and small notes, with issuance limited after the China conflict.
